There are several buildings of architectural note grouped in the courtyard, but the great hall or mahamandapa, in front of the main shrine, is the glory of the place, and one of the most magnificent buildings in Vijayanagar. It is open on three sides, and supported on piers, so arranged, that they leave a large hall in the centre, and a smaller one on each of the three open sides. The outer piers are cut out of immense monolithic blocks of granite, covered with carved ornament and mythological figures, and with clusters of small shafts grouped around the central column. This building has evidently attracted the special attention of the Muhammadan invaders in their attempts to destroy the buildings of the city, of which this was no doubt regarded as one of the most important, for, though many of the other temples show traces of the action of fire, in none of them are the effects so marked as in this. EXPLORATION AND RESEARCH. ■¥ The record of the past season in exploration has been one of good forward progress, and it affords me no little satisfaction to be able to state that the prospects of work in this field are each year becoming brighter. Exploration, as I have explained in previous Reports, has been bound to take but a second place in the official programme while there were so many arrears of conservation work to be swept off. Now, however, that so much has been done to make up for the neglect of past years in respect of conservation, we can look forward in the near future to making the ex- cavation of buried monuments as much an integral part of the year’s programme as the preservation of monuments already known. A uniform policy in this respect can- not, of course, be taken up at once and simultaneously in all the Circles ; for in some of them conservation is still very backward, and, moreover, it must be remembered that this is the first time that excavations on scientific lines have been seriously attempted in this country, and that both time and patience are required to train up the local staffs to the methods of competent European explorers. A good beginning, however, has now been made, and the results already obtained make it sufficiently apparent that there is little cause for the pessimism so often expressed as to the possibilities of excavation in India. Indeed, it may confidently be affirmed — and I say it after due reflection — that in a few years’ time India will be able to boast of sites of the early historic period as complete in themselves and as instructive, relatively, as any unearthed in the Nearer East. Prominent among the sites that have been taken systematically in hand is that of Kasia — a spot which Sir A. Cunningham long ago identified with the famous Kugi- nagara or Kusinara, the traditional scene of Buddha’s nirvana. Sir A. Cunningham’s identification was, in the first instance, based on the indications as to the position of the spot offered by the Chinese pilgrims, but in 1875-6 his assistant, Mr. Carlleyle, unearthed among the ruins of Kasia a colossal image of the recumbent Buddha, which appeared to agree with the one described by Hiuen Thsang. Such circumstantial evidence naturally gave strong support to Sir A. Cunningham’s theory, particularly as no other image of a similar kind was known to exist in all northern India ; nay, it was accepted by everyone as conclusive proof of the identity of the two places, and the question was regarded as settled up to a few years ago, when Mr. V. A NEW TYPE OF POTTERY FROM BALUCHISTAN. The small collection of vases, of which I am here publishing some selected specimens, derive some considerable interest from the fact that, as far as is at present known, they are quite unique of their kind. They were obtained about a year ago through the instrumentality of Mr. Hughes Duller, I.C.S., from a mound ^ near the little village of Nal situated in the Jhalawan district of the Kalat State, approximately in lat. 27° 40' and long. 66° 14'.® A few of the vases had been found quite accidentally by peasants from Nal digging earth for their fields, and were recovered from them by the Gazetteer official on the spot, Mirza Sher Muhammad, who afterwards, with the permission of the chief of the Bizanjo tribe, had a small excavation made in the side of the mound, and procured as many other specimens as he could, without unduly exciting the inquisitiveness of the peasants. The Sohr damb mound, in which the pottery was unearthed, lies actually at a distance of miles north-east of Nal village, in an alluvial plain adjoining the skirts of the hills. It is of clay, strewn with pieces of pottery and burnt bricks. Actual measurements of the mound were not taken on the spot, but Mirza Sher Muhammad states that, so far as he can recollect, its height above the surrounding country was about 30 feet and its diameter about 50 feet, and that the pottery was discovered about 5 feet from the ground level. There are five other mounds of the same description within a radius of about 150 yards from the Sohr damb. Several other mounds, some of which look like the ruins of old mud forts, lie in the Nal valley within a distance of five miles, the principal among which are the Khayan, Tazi Karkakan and Tegha dambs.® No other antiquities of any sort were found along with the pottery, nor was there anything about the mound itself which could afford a clue to its origin or date. I must state at the outset, before describing the pottery, that I have not, myself, had an opportunity of examining the whole of it. The collection consists of 59 pieces in all, and only a representative selection of these could be sent to me at Simla. I have had, however, the advantage of seeing photographs of practically all the other pieces of any interest, besides coloured illustrations of a dozen of them. The thumb and index finger of the right hand, the palm of which is turned to the front, are joined and touch the little finger of the left hand. This gesture is one of the conven- tional attitudes {mudras) of the Buddha and expresses the expounding of the sacred law {dharmacakra-mudra). RUINED TEMPLE IN THE NURPUR FORT. NORPUR lies in latitude 32° 18' 10" north, and longitude 75° 5 s' 30" east, on the- Jabhar Khad, a small tributary of the Chakki torrent which flows into the Bias It is picturesquely situated on a spur, 2,000 feet above the sea-level, and some twenty-two miles north-west of Kangra It was formerly the capital of a petty hill state ruled by the Pathaniya clan of the Rajputs For long it has enjoyed a considerable com- mercial importance dependent on the manufacture of shawls, and the fact of its being a great rendezvous on the way to Kashmir, Chamba and Ladakh But now it presents a somewhat depopulated appearance, which has resulted from the collapse of the shawl trade.^ With the addition of the taluk^s of Shahpur and Kandi Bachertu, now attached to the district of Gurdaspur, and of a small tract across the Ravi, that was given in exchange to the Raja of Jammu, the boundaries of the old principality are retained almost entire in the present ta

niature temples, which are in a good state of preservation. Two gates to the east, forming the main entrances to the fort, are also extant. The rest, except the portion now used as a School building and Post Office with Public Works Department rest- house, obviously erected after the British conquest, is all in ruins. The fort, along with several other strongholds in the district, was blown up in A.D. 1857. By far the most interesting building in the fort is the ruined temple that was excavated in 1886 by the late Mr. C. J. Rodgers, Archaeological Surveyor to the Punjab Government. As we learn from bis manuscript report for the months May to January 1886, it was merely a mound before excavation and covered with flowers and the dSbris of some British officer’s bungalow. A moulded stone, which Mr. Rodgers noticed under these remains, led him to the supposition that the mound contained some ancient building. On excavation, he discovered the basement of a large temple pro- fusely decorated with carving, besides a number of sculptured fragments, which once belonged to its upper portion. The exhumation, however, was not completed, as a later structure was still left masking the north-eastern portion of the base with its mouldings and carvings. In March 1904, at the suggestion of Dr. Vogel, this struc- ture was dismantled by the late Mr. Farley, Executive Engineer, Kahgra. The space round the temple was also widened out, and thus all the decorative details on the base- ment were exposed and made accessible to the camera. This temple is 117 feet long and 50 feet wide externally. It is built of red sand- stone and consists of an ante-room {mandapa) leading through a central chamber {antaralaya) to the sanctuary {garbhagrha) octagonal in plan with recesses at the angles. Its plan does not resemble that of any other shrine in the Punjab, but is very similar to those of the famous temples of Govind dev at Bindraban and Haridev at Govardhan near Mathura (Muttra).^ The main entrance must have been at the south end, though there were entrances direct into the central room on the east and west sides as is the case in the Haridev temple. But now the stairs are extant on the west side only. That it had entrances at the south and east sides is evidenced by the stones that are still preserved and shaped like those found on the thresholds inside the temple. The east and west sides of the mandapa are open, and the inner surface, from which the stone pavement was probably removed, is enclosed on the east and west sides by a colonnade consisting of two rows of two double pilasters and pillars. The complete bases of the latter are still extant. The ornamentation preserved on the bases of the pilasters (see Plate XXXVIII) shows a marked similarity in design to some of the early Mugha-l buildings in the Lahore Fort.* The shafts, probably square in form, supported either double arches or lintels provided with brackets, such as have been found among the dibris Plate XXXIX). Unlike Maheth described above, Saheth falls entirely within the limits of the Bahraich district, being situated about half a mile to the west of the boundary line of the districts of Gonda and Bahraich, and only a furlong to the south of the Balrampur- ikauna road. The more conspicuous part of the mound at the present day is 1,600 feet long from the north-east corner to the south-west and varies in width from 450 feet to 700 feet, but that it formerly extended for several hundred feet further in the eastern direction, is proved by the general elevation of the lands lying to the east of Saheth and the fact that a large ruin marked H in General Cunningham’s plan,^ and identified after him by Dr. Hoey with a stiifa of Sariputta, is still connected with the main site by raised ground.^ The average elevation of Saheth is 14 feet above the level of surrounding fields. It contains, however, a large number of eminences which rose much higher. Twenty of these were excavated by General Cunningham in 1863 and 1877-8, and revealed temples, stupas and other structures, to each of which he affixed a number from i to 18. Dr. Hoey’s operations were much more extensive, since not only did he open every detached mound that he noticed, but also led long trenches throughout the length and breadth of the site. We need not, therefore, be surprised if he could not complete any of the buildings that he commenced. It is also obvious that he suffered from insufficiency of funds, for he invariably left the excavated debris either on the buildings themselves or quite close to them. These heaps of rubbish had ver}^ much hardened in the course of time, and their removal naturally entailed much waste of time and money, which could have been fruitfully utilized elsewhere. During the past season, work was restricted to only those of the more important structures which had been left unfinished by the previous explorers. The materials now at our disposal seem to indicate that the use of Sanskrit in inscriptions originated in Mathura.^ This would also account for its early adoption in the west of India, for there must have existed a close connection between the west- ern Satraps and those of Mathura. At the same time, the masonry of these platforms was repaired, and vast heaps of accumulated debris removed from outside the entrance, a measure which has immeasurably enhanced the imposing aspect of this Gateway. Tn comparison with the expenditure on Muhammadan Monuments, the cost of repairs to Hindu and Buddhist Monuments in the Northern Circle has been rela- tively small, amounting to Rs, 1,011 in the Punjab and Rs. 12,960 in the United Provinces. The most important monuments in the repairer’s hands were the recently excavated remains at Saheth-Maheth, the brick temple at Tinduli, three shrines at Brindaban and the Dhamekh Stupa at Sarnath. With regard to the last mentioned, the massive ashlar stone work round the drum of the stipe has been admirably rebuilt by the Public Works Department at the points where it had begun to buckle outwards, but the new cap of glaring white plaster on the summit is anything but satisfactory. The advice tendered by Dr, Vogel when officiating Director-General was to the effect that the outer courses of brick work should be removed, the core well grouted and plastered over to prevent the percolation of rain water, and the outer bricks then replaced. Arrangements are now being made for the ugly new capping to he removed and for Dr. Vogel's instructions to be carried out. I mentioned last year that the newly excavated courtyard at 'lakht-i-Bahi, Frontier which contains some fine stucco relievos in excellent preservation, was to be i tected by a roof of reinforced concrete. Detailed plans for the construction of this Bn Western Circle, t roof were prepared by the Garrison Engineer, Risalpur, but it was subsequently found that the use of reinforced concrete was precluded owing to the difficulty of obtaining a sufficient supply of water on the summit of the hill, and accordingly fresh plans and estimates had to be prepared by the Assistant Commanding Royal Engineer, Nowshera. In the meantime, further clearance has been carried out among the minor ruins to the east and south of the main structure and seyeral well executed sculptures brought to light, including two relievos mm sifu, as well as a cinerary urn. Considering the vast number and importance of the ancient monuments in Western India, the annual allotment made for their upkeep by the Local Govern- ment is unduly small, and as the claims of conservation increase, it becomes less and less adequate to the needs of the Presidency. So far, however, as funds, Provincial or Imperial would permit, the progress made during the past year has been steady and substantial. At Nasik, effective drainage has been provided for the Pandu Lena Caves by lowering the level of the ground outside and providing catch- water gutters on the rock face above the caves with cross gutters at intervals to carry off the rain water. Masonry pillars, too, have been constructed in several of the caves to support the roof, and Cave XIX, which was excavated during the reign of the Satavahana King, Krishna, has been cleared of the deep accumulation of debris which was choking it. The well known groups of monuments at Agra, Fatehpur and other important centres, where responsible officers either of the Public Werks Department or of the Archeological Department have been constantly on the spot, have been most admirably repaired. HE total sum of Rs. 3,04,816 was expended on the conservation of ancient monu- | ments throughout British India in the year 1917-18. This figure is to be com- pared with Rs. 3,10,736 for the year preceding, but this latter figure itself represented a decrease of some Rs. 16,000 in the figures for 1915-16. It is hoped, however, that the downward tendency thus disclosed will be arrested, now that the War is happily over, and that normal expenditure will be both restored and m4iintained, There is no activity of Government to which the dictum that a “a stitch in time saves nine” is more applicable than to the upkeep of its ancient monuments. Even as it is, and despite the War, the falling off in most Provinces is very slight, while in some cases actual increases are shown, for example in the Delhi Province, with an expenditure of Rs. 59.940 in 1917-18 against Rs. 41,121 the year before; or the Central Provinces which this year records Rs, 13,432 against a previous Rs, 9,614, On the whole, there- fore, it may be justly claimed that the policy of Government in regard to the preser- vation of those memorials of the past which it has inherited from its predecessors has been quite well maintained, considering the phenomenal difficulties of the las

The country is not very favourable for archeological exploration, for on the one hand the enormous distances between one village and another make travelling slow and difficult; and on the other owing to the general dearth of stone there are few architectural or sculptural monuments note and importance. Indeed, outside of the city of Bikaner only one temple of substantial construction has so far been discovered in this tract, viz.,—the Jaina temple of Susini at Morkhina‘—and scattered fragments of two or three others have been found at Palta*; apart from these, all the lithic monuments found in the district are sati-tablets, hirtistambhas, and chhattris. Sati-tablets are so common in the southern part of the Bikaner State that there is hardly a village without a few of them. But in the northern part of the State they are entirely unknowv, The oldest examples were found at Bhadla and Morkhana (12th century A.D.), Rasisar, Kanvalisar (13th—l4th century), and Chh4par (13th century), and these refer to Chhikana, Sankhala, and Mohila Rajputs, respectively. Two or three safi-tablets referring to Chiefs of note who played a prominent part in the Rathor colonization of Bikaner at the end of the 15th and the beginning of the 16th century A.D., were found in the tract of the desert to the south of the capital. Though of little value archeo- logically, the sati-tablets are of considerable importance from the point of view of local history and of the history of Rajputana in general. Dr. Tessitori has been able to illustrate the examples found fully and exhaustively. Thanks to the information gained by Dr. Tessitori from local chronicles he has been able to identify the heroes of the majority of these Sati memorials and to use the monuments as a means of amplifying his history. Hundreds of sati-tablets referring to Pallival brahmins and dating from the 16th century onwards, were found in villages to the west of Gajner, but these are of less historical interest. Dr. Tessitori explains the sati-tablet as a monument of the Rajputs par excel- lence, which in Northern Rajputana came into vogue towards the beginning of the 12th century A.D. Before this time, according to him the function of the sati- tablets was fulfilled by the gévardhana. Further excavations at Nigarjunikonda have not yielded finds of apecial importance, though some of the reliefs found during the four years under review are again of the same high artistie quality as the sculptures found previously at that ancient Buddhist. site, The operations at another Buddhist site, viz., Paharpur in Bengal, the ancient monastery of Somapura, were brought to a suocessful conclusion during the period under review. Here a monastery of really enormous dimensions, and built according to a splendidly conceived plan, has been entirely laid bare, and Readers will find a detailed description of the results, with a fine site-plan, in the present volume. Included with it is a report by Mr Dtksair on the excavation at Satyapir Bhitf, an adjoining mound, where a Temple of Tara, with many minor structures erected around it, has been discovered, Excavations have also been carried on at the ancient Buddhist seat of learning, Nalandi, where three more sites have been attacked with very satis- factory results. Among the minor finds uncovered among these ruins was a hoard of hundreds of bronze images representing Buddhas, Bodhisattvas and divinities of the Northern Buddhist pantheon, of great interest for the atudy of medimval Indian art. These bronzes have been fully illustrated in the plates accompanying this volume, and a deseription will be found under the heading ‘Museums’. Reference may be made here of a somewhat similar find of bronze images made at Kurkihar which Readers will find discussed under Section VIT: ‘Treasure Trove’. The importance of these two finds cannot be exagge: ated, especially in view of the fact that a number of these images are provided with inseriptions, some of which are dated. Maung Mya carried out a number of excavations in Burma, La XXIX especially in and around Pagan, that locality so rich in antiquarian remains of the middle-ages. All scholars and lovers of Indian art will he interested in the series of remarkable wall-paintings discovered by Maung Mya, and illustrated in the coloured Frontispiece and a number of plates at the end of the Second Part, These al secco paintings (many of which represent Hindu gods) in three temples in and around Pagan carry back the history of painting in Burma to the ith century A.p., thus to a period from which not a single wall-painting was known before. The repairs done at the cost of Maharaja Manindra Chandra Nandi Bahadur, of Cossimbazar, amounted to Rs. 2,650 and were carried out by the Maharaja's (5 ) Mining Surveyor. They have been done creditably, but some further repairs seemed to be needed. I suggested that the alasa of one of the temples should be renewed, as it is broken and not in keeping with the remaining parts of the building; that the statues of Siva’s Bull, which now lie loose inside the temple area, should be put upon stone pedestals facing the entrances of the temples; that the broken statues now lying outside sbould be placed upon a platform inside the fencing of temple area, in order to prevent their being taken away; and that the ground around the two eastern temples should be levelled, so that rain water may not collect there and do damage to the walls. Ihave been informed by Government that the Maharaja of Cossimbazar has been asked through the Commissioner of Burdwan to have these additional repairs executed, and that he has agreed to do so. The temple of Kalyanesvari seems to attract a great number of local people, who come there and offer goats to the goddess, a form of Durga. It is evidently a recent building and not of much archeological interest. The principal temple is a square with a pyramidal roof and a hall in front, covered by a vault. The image, I was told, is so thickly covered with red paint that it was quite undistinguishable. The temple court is surrounded by open halls, houses for the Sebaits, and besides has five small shrines with Mahadevas, marked by spires, one of which is now empty. The best part of the building is the shrine in the south-western corner. Its spire rests upon an ornamented band containing in its northern side figures of Siva and connected deities ; to the east are images of the Avataras of Vishnu, and to the south and west figures of men and women, mostly obscene. ‘I'he carvings around the door are of the later Bengali style. The main temple and the other shrines are now covered with whitewash. The walls in places had battlements, but these never seem to have been carried on all along the line of the walls. The outer court to the south is connected with the inner one by an open portico resting on pillars, and has two small shrines inside. The buildings are generally of stone, but in some places bricks have been used. Their preservation is fair, and I observed only one or two cracks in the walls. A portion of the wall of the outer court has fallen, and this part as also some of the broken battlements should be restored by the Sebaits. Close to the temple is another small shrine, consisting merely of a brick tower. The surroundings of these temples, which stand on the bank of a small tributary of the Barakar river, are perhaps the most attractive part of this group of ancient remains. DISTRICT BANKURA. 3. The temples at Vishnupur—From a historical point of view, perhaps the most curious fact in connection with the Malla Rajas of Vishnupur is that they used a separate era of their own, called Malla Saka in the inscriptions. I have not found any information about this era either in Prinsep’s Useful Tables or in Cunningham’s Book of Indian Eras. In one only of the temple inscriptions the equivalent of Malla Saka 1064 is given as Saka 1680, and thus the difference between the Malla Era and the Bengali Sal appears to be exactly one hundred years. I suspect that the Malla year in other respects entirely followed the Fasli year of Bengal, and that the Rajas of Vishnupur, out of vain glory, merely reduced the Bengali year by one hundred in order to establish a special era of their own. But this conjecture remains to be verified, and I shall try to get copies of the old records of the Vishnupur Rajas, dated in the Malla Era, which = said e be still in existence and which perhaps will afford some clue to solve this puzzle, ho judge from the dates of the templ

The remains at\ Bagerhai.—The tomb of Khan Jahan and the Sat Gumbaz were inspected by me in the company of the Executive Engineer, Circular and Eastern Canals Division, in order to settle what repairs were needed. The estimate prepared by the Executive Engineer amounts to Rs, 15,410 and has been sanctioned by Government. The tomb isin fair order, and requires only petty repairs, Unfortunately the floor of glazed tiles, which was the most attractive feature of the building cannot be restored, as most of the tiles have been taken away. Some well-preserved specimens are in the Indian Museum, and others are placed around the stone sarcophagus. Recent experiments at Gaur huve shown that it is at present impossible in India to produce glazed tiles to match the old ones. The prevailing colours are white and blue, and the shape is hexagonal. 7 ; As regards the history of Khan Jahan, which is so densely wrapt up by legend, the only fact, besides the date of his death and burial contained in the inscriptions on his tomb, is that perhaps mention is made of him as the builder of a mosque in an inscription from Dacca, which has been edited by Blochmann. It has been pointed out by that scholar that the Khwaja Jahan of this inscrip- tion may be identical with him. The inscription refers to the reign of the Bengal Sultan Mahmud Shah I. and its date (13th June, 1459 A.D.) is a little earlier than the death of Khan Jahan (end of October, 1459 A.D.). The popular traditions about Khan Jahan have recently been collected in a pamphlet published by Mr. D. Sunder, the Commissioner in the Sundarbans, but they deserve no faith whatever. The Sat Gumbaz mosque is of very inferior workmanship as compared with the tomb of Khan Jahan. Owing to this it has suffered greatly from the effects of time, and is in a bad state of repairs. It has been decided to preserve it oaly asa partial ruin, so as to show what the building was like when complete. And even this will be an expensive matter, as it includes a great deal of masonry work and such other repairs as will prevent further decay. Evidently the building has suffered very much from ‘the dampness of the Sundarbans climate, and it has been decided to make the ground around the mosque sloping, to prevent rain water from collecting around it, and to pro- vide for drains. The floor inside the mosque is exceedingly moist, and it would be best if it could be covered all over with asphalt. This unfortunately being too expensive, it has been decided to provide anew macadamised flooring. To procure a better view of the building from outside all the trees around it have to be cut down, and the area will be fenced off. The compensation to be paid for the trees, most of which are betelnut trees, amounts to some five hundred rupees, DISTRICT RAJSHAHI. 7. The ancient mosque at Bagha.—This mosque is built on the same plan as the Tantipara mosque at Gaur and the dimensions of both agree very close- ly. It is an oblong building, divided by a row of stone pillars into two aisles, (9 ) each of which was covered by five hemispherical domes. It has five arched openings in front, corresponding to the prayer-niches in the back wall. Beginning from south, the place of the fourth niche was occupied by the pulpit, andin the north-western corner was the zenana platform with only one small mihrab. Both externally and internally the walls are adorned with brick ornamentation of no mean order, although not quite as graceful as in the Tantipara mosque. The. mosque was built by Nusrat Shah, the son of Husain Shah, King of Bengal, in the Hijri year 930 or 1523-1524 A.D. The inscrip- tion slab has fallen down, but is preserved inside the mosque. As the mosque is described in the inscription as ‘ masjid-i-jami’ or ‘cathedral mosque’, it must have been considered a building of some im

Rupa, amongst many other things, means‘ painting,’ and that it must be taken in this sense, becomes at once evident, if one looks up to the roof of the cave, where indeed the traces of old wall paintings, crude and weather worn though they are, still can be observed. The preceding lines mention a certain Sutanuka, a Devadasi (Sutanuka nama devadasikyt), and we must expect that the remainder either says that she caused the cave to be excavated or that what follows tells us the story depicted on the roof just above the inscription, in which Sutanuka played a certain part. ; We thus have in this cave remains of painting, more than 2000 years old, peoeely the oldest ever found in India. Crude though the remains of the resco now look, a closer inspection reveals that it is really old work, no mere modern scrawling. ‘We observe in many places the ancient chaitya window, so characteristic for old Indian Art. A two-wheeled carriage drawn by three or four horses is just like similar ones in the relievos of Sanchi or Bharhut. Even the human figures bear a distinct antique type. The figures are painted in a sort of crimson upon a white ground. Men, elephants, trees alike have the same colour. Only the outlines are sketched in | black, and the eyes are left white, while the hair is black, and sometimes tied into a nod to the left, a fashion which still survives in that part of the country. Clothing is shown in white, with red outlines, while the head, hands and feet are of the usual colour, The various scenes are arranged in .semi- circular pannels, divided by red lines. The lowest band is yellow with red. Whether there is any connection between those scenes, is at present impossible ( 14 ) to say. Iam likewise unable to offer any explanation of the stories, which the frescos may represent. ButI have no doubt that my statment with regard to the date of these wall paintings will remain substantially true. ° Unfortunately, it was almost impossible to get photographs giving some clear idea of these interesting paintings, and I am afraid I shall have to go there a second time, to get a coloured tracing. The opening words of the Sitabenga cave inscription are likewise clear. They must be translated: ‘ poets venerable by nature kindle the heart,’ for this is the simplest meaning of the words: adipayanti hadayam sabhava-garu-kavayo. The remainder is doubtful, but in an inscription beginning thus one must expect some further praise of the charms of poetry. If this be accepted, the next question will be: why was this inscription put up in this cave? The most natural answer to this seems to me: because the building had some connection with poetry. It was a hall where theatrical plays were acted, poems recited, and similar exhibitions held. ; From its style the building seems eminently suited to this purpose. Hemis- pherical benches cut out of the rock rise in tiers, overlooking a platform in front, which is sufficiently large for the erection of a small stage. Small passages have been made between the different rows, and radiating lines divide this miniature amphitheatre into several blocks. These lines have been described by previous visitors as drains, but as there are no openings, water could only collect in them. To the right small steps lead up to the upper chamber, which is cbiong, with broad benches all along the walls. This was evidently used at night, when the cold of the winter invited to seek shelter inside. In front are still the holes in the rock, into which fitted the wooden posts that held the curtain. In front of the inner benches was space enough for a small ‘nautch’ party. The amphitheatre down below was able to seat about fifty persons. It struck me that there might be some connection or analogy between these interruptions in this darker stratum and our subsidiary circles, and I proceeded to make a fresh examination of the former. My growing suspicion was confirmed. They were not clear cuts through the several strata, neither were they cup-like depressions in them. The former would have shown us the ends of the dark belt to right and left of the break clean cut and horizontal. In the latter alternative, the dark belt would not have been really broken at all, but would merely have sagged, and would have been found to extend continuously beneath the cup. What we actually observed was essentially different from either. The dark belt was really broken, but the severed end, instead of stopping short horizontally, swept downwards in two sharp curves which rapidly passed into parallel vertical lines. And it was apparent that the break had filled by the settling into it of the higher strata. Examination of the bases then settled the question definitely by disclos- ing semicircles in the horizontal plane at the foot of the vertical section. On deepening the plane so as to get a complete section, its form was ascertained _ to be a vertical tongue, the widening root of which was upwards, the slightly rounded tip a few feet below the level of the floor.- ; In considering these phenomena it was then necessary to bear in mind the following points. The subsidiary circles which we had first met, and which measured about two feet in diameter, were evidently counterparts of those discovered at the foot of these depressions or breaks where we could see a vertical surface. It was thus probable that there had been similar phenomena in the soil above our subsidiary circles, which for one reason or another we had not previously observed. The reason for this failure on our part to notice them also seemed clear. The soil above the floor was all Ganges silt for some 8 feet. Any cavity that might have filled within this area would have filled with material of like nature to that of the sides of the cavity. In digging from above, therefore, and’ working on horizontal planes only, this filling had at no time been visible to the eye until we reached a level lower than the bottom limit of the silt. At 18 feet we were working in the red subsoil. Here the Ganges silt which had filled the cavity from above was clearly differentiated by its colour from the soil composing the sides of the orifice, and thus the round tongue of silt became visible when the horizontal plane was cleared, and showed up in the form of these dark circles. With the second miniature Talar, the whole gains that element of height which is essential for its dignity. Without it it is as archi- tecturally inconceivable as before. But all details are missing; the eye cannot, and probably never could, on this small seal, detect sculptures between the various storeys. But this would be demand- ing the impossible. So far as it goes the seal is quite sufficient evidence for the fact that people in ancient India knew of three-storeyed structures with miniatures of themselves upon their roofs. And where can such structures be now pointed to, save in the sculptures of Per

But then the Commissioner of the Patna Division, Mr. Oldham, who has so repeatedly assisted me by his advice, suggested that I try to line my pits with corrugated iron. The Superintending Engineer agreed that this was safe enough, if we could sink it to the depths required. I ordered rings and excavation was renewed. But it was well on in June before the operations could be started. The season’s showers have meant delay, and as I write the well is not completed. The test must be post- poned now after all! I cannot say, though, that our excavations have been wholly fruitless. Both they and our borings have brought to light stray broken potsherds at extraordinary depths, one at 53 feet below the surface of the ground. These potsherds seem a certain proof that my idea of sinkage must be right. For otherwise how explain their presence at these depths? “ They could have got to these positions by falling down a hole or by following slowly on some sinking object. No other explanation seems conceivable. But meanwhile though we are entitled to take courage from these scraps, the recovery of an actual statue is deferred. Another point of interest and importance disclosed to us while search- ing for our minor circles is what appears to be the unexpected size of our pillard hall. It has been found that these subsidiary circles extend uninterruptedly to a point. far beyond our established pillars on the east, and also far beyond those on the west. From this J can infer one thing alone, namely that pillars once existed here which now have sunk or been removed and left no trace. This is easily possible on the east at least. As -we have seen above the Gupta people in their levelling destroyed the ash- stratum in thisarea. There thus were left no ashes here to form those funnels in the soil which served to locate pillars in the area west of this. The same thing may conceivably have happened on the west as well. But there the columns sinking have left traces after all. We find for instance circles of dark clay like our subsidiary circles, but of slightly larger size, in the posi- tion of the 14th row of pillars from the first known row along the eastern edge. No corresponding traces of main columns have been met yet on the east, but little of this area has been examined. It appears probable though that.15 was the total number of columns in our row instead of 10. And the occurrence of a brick wall east and west along the north side of our site at just the distance seemingly required for 15 columns tends towards confirma- tion of this theory. Does this then tend to threaten the resemblance between our hall and the throne-room of Darius? On the contrary it appears if anything to strengthen it. . What has been said above about the use of Indian cubits instead of Achezmenian ones in regard to the spacing of the pillars stands as evident fact. Our pillars are ten Indian cubits each from each, the Persian pillars are ten Persian cubits. These are simple facts. But it will have been noticed probably that this equation of the varying cubits does not apparently apply to surface measurements. Precise exactitude is not yet possible, but such distances as can be ascertained are too nearly identical with the Persepolitan to admit of any difference

The paral- lelism between the two is thus sufficiently exact, and it becomes the more significant when we remember that with one exception the throne-room at Persepolis is the largest building of the ancient world. It is not as though the scale were a mere average one, which might be common to innumerable examples anywhere. The size has hitherto been held unique. If then our hall so closely oo it even in this regard, is not the assumption of a borrowing strengthened by the fact ? : 70 The final proof is still outstanding here as in so many other cases. But every present indication points this way. And be it noted that this greater size brings the position of our pillared hall into even better relation than before to the mound at Site No.2. The resemblance was close enough for practical purposes before. It becomes closer still with a hall the same size as the Persian one. Turning now to such trial measures as we have been enabled to carry out. at our new sites, I will record first of all the fact that a trial trench begun on the north of Site No. 2 before the opposition of the land-owners was made known to me, had to be abandoned, and opportunity did not offer for a resump- tion of this work in this year under review. Site No. 2 thus lies out of our present reckoning altogether. At Site No.3 we were more fortunate. This is the mound whose external configuration agrees with such striking fidelity to the theory of a mound over such a building as the Persepolitan hypothesis would locate at this spot. The main body of the mound and even its southern lips are so given over to Muhammadan graves that no digging of any kind was possible in these portions of the site, which constitute of course the bulk of it. But the wide terrace on the north was under different ownership, and instead of being given over to graves was planted as a mango orchard. At first the owner very courteously permitted us to begin a few trial trenches at this spot, but subsequently this permission even was withdrawn, and it was not until into March that work could be undertaken even here with anything like serious intention. It will be obvious that this was far too late for us to accomplish much this season. I sank a series of parallel trial trenches running north and south, and these have enabled me to form some idea of the stratification here while preserving the actual strata. They show us two fairly superficial layers of brick remains, one of medizval date apparently, the other possibly of Kushan times, while abundant indica- tions have been met to prove that the original monument goes back to Mauryan times. This of itself isa matter of no small moment. There have been some- thing like 23 centuries in which, if the position of this mound with relation ‘to the others were mere accident, the accident in question might have occurred. The trial excavations show that this is not the case. There certainly was a Mauryan building at this spot, presumably contemporary with the pillared hall. This much of the general design then is assured as Mauryan, and this constitutes a clear step in advance, although it does not prove anything in regard to our main enquiry. We have numerous fragments of polished stone which must be Mauryan and a few of those exceptionally large and massive bricks assignable only to this period. And at a great depth, we have a belt of bright blue clay which yielded us the anticipated bits of wood in the one trial pit we were enabled to sink this year. The most striking feature of these fragments though, is the fact that at this site the Mauryan stone shows regularly flat surfaces and sharp right-angle corners. At the old site all our fragments had curved surfaces, showing them to be broken bits of monolithic columns. Here the conditions are radically different and our fragments seem more in the nature of facing stones. ‘All of them are small, and most of them are wholly plain. Some few are carved,

of any careful or important epigraph. Rude chisellings are all they seem to be. But were these chisellings devoid of meaning? That seems somehow improbable to me. 74 The trench, however, has not yet disclosed the provenance of these stone fragments, nor have we any sign of any surface to which an epigraph could be affixed. It has though yielded us odd finds of interest, fragments of pottery with glazed or enamelled surfaces of green and blue and yellow, where the enamel, in the course of time, has quite disintegrated and is hard to pick from the embedding earth, and two gold coins. These are the first gold pieces our excavations have recovered, and it is matter of no little interest that both are of the Kushan type, one Vasuveda and one later King. The Kushan evidences at Kumrahar appear of unexpected frequency. In concluding this Report I must needs stress the fact that we are as yet upon the very threshhold. of our work. The superficial and the deeper resemblances to the Persepolitan platform are actual, as I state them. But it is manifest that these resemblances may after all prove purely accidental. To my mind sucha chain of. accidents is weéll-nigh inconceivable, I must confess; but it would be unpardonably rash to claim that we have really confess; but it would be unpardonably rash to claim that we have really proved as yet that any Mauryan replica exists. It seems most highly probable as I go to press, but further excavation is imperative before we know for certain. The work is in its very infancy as yet. D. B. RATAN TATA’S EXCAVATIONS AT PATALIPUTRA. On my return io Pataliputra early in December 1914, I found, as was to be expected, that the entire excavated area at Site No. I, the position of the pillared hall, was under water and presented the appearance of an extensive tank, of whose depth I was only too well aware. ‘Ihe :same condi- tions had existed at the commencement of the previous year’s work, and we had nevertheless been enabled, later on, to extend our digging very materially, as was detailed in my Report for that season. But the situation this year was more serious. Practically all of our efforts in the spring of 1914 had been directed toward deepening the excavation (apart from our endeavour to determine the extent of the palace), in order to permit of. our locating and drawing as many of the subsidiary circles as possible, for the completion of the ground plan of the structure, and these operations had inevitably lowered the level of the whole area very considerably. In the previous year so much water had accumulated in the monsoon that it was only far on in the season that work could be resumed at this site, and this year it seemed doubtful if the site would dry at all. The fear was only too well founded. Not until well into June was the floor of the excavation sufficiently dry to permit of a man walking on it, and the result was, that no new work could be undertaken. It is manifest that until adequate pumping arrangements can be made, conti- nuation of the exploratory work at this site is impracticable. This year we had no. pumps, and in. consequence could do no work. But, curiously enough, this does not mean to say that 3 no progress has been made as regards the problems raised by this particular site. Very distinct progress has been made, in at least two directions, even here; and such progress as to reduce our outstanding problems of this structure to a comparatively small residuum. It will be remembered that for our understanding of the site and our reconstruction of the vanished palace, we are thrown back upon a minute scrutiny of the soil and a synthetic study of its stratification. One of the most singular features of this stratification is the deep belt of apparently virgin soil which has been found to intervene between the layer of black ashes (which lies seven or eight feet deep), and the thin belt of blue clay which marks the position of the original floor, now some 16 feet’ below the surface. When this virgin belt was first met with, and the existence underneath it of a lower level of occupation was determined, there seemed no way of explaining the paradox except by assuming that at some period a flood must have covered the original floor, and deposited this thickness of virgin soil upon it. I accordingly made this assumption provisionally, but was at pains ‘to’ explain in the Report of the second season that the question of such a flood was not primarily an archeological one, and that the tenableness or otherwise of this detail of my general synthesis was largely immaterial from the strictly archeological point of view. It was known from the strati- fication around the Asoka column at Bakhra, across the Ganges, that a great flood must have occurred at some early period, and this made my

ugh to explain why it was that the simple pits or wells which we excavated in the endeavour to overtake them were doomed to failure from the commencement. Our wells were outlined immediately above the particular subsidiary circle, with the centre of the well coincident with thé centre of the circle, and they were of course taken down vertically. The sculputres, however, were not sinking in this vertical fashion at all, but with a certain amount of inclination to one side or the other, and thus we never could have reached them in this way, however deep we might have gone. Tt will be observed that. incidentally the theory of sinkage is confirmed. Originally the columns and sculptures stood on the top of the stylobate, some- thing lke eight feet below the present surface of ihe ground, and thus there could have been absolutely no trace of either at a depth of 17 to 47 18 feet if they. had not come down through the soil to this lower level. The big stone head, it will be recalled, was recovered several feet below the proper floor, although we did not know it at the time. Thus the determination of the fact that in reality no flood had taken place, and the consequent reconsideration of the problem and the evidences, have resulted in our advancing very appreciably in our understanding of the site, without any extension of the actual excavation. Nor is this the only direction in which progress has been made even: at this particular site. Apart from the all important discovery of the terrace at Kumrahar and its superficial coincidences with the terrace at Persepolis, the most striking feature of my last-year’s Report was the interpretation there offered of the subsidiary circles at Site No. I and the consequent inference that the struc- ture under excavation had been in reality, not only a palace corresponding to the Throne-room at Persepolis, but a Throne-room of that specifically Ache- menian type which is disclosed by the sculptured facsade of Darius’s tomb, and represented in the bas-reliefs on the entrances to this very Hall of a Hundred Columns itself. ‘Phe ‘‘ Talar theory ” was one of the salient features of the whole Report, and, it is to be apprehended, that. portion also which will have taxed most markedly the credulity of the reader. It was an idea which in and of itself was.doomed to appear at first sight as trenching rather closely on the fanciful, and I was so conscious of this that nothing but thé clearest possible stratigraphical evidences, and the direct confirmation of my views which was afforded me by the recovery of our large head in the pro- phesied position, vould have induced me to put such a theory forth. But I saw no possible escape from that conclusion, and the head afforded confirma- tion enough. I will now record that further most unexpected confirmation has been found, and confirmation which, to my own mind, at least, denermincs the question affirmatively once for all. In the course of certain literary studies which I was prompted to make while on leave, by the suggestive evidences at Kumarhar, I found striking reason to believe that the very group of palaces which are now in course of excavation are specifically referred to and, in a very general way, described in the pages of the Mahabharata, where they are ascribed to supernatural agency in the person of the famous Asura Maya. In a paper entitled “The Zoroastrian period of Indian History,” published in tlhe January number of the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (1915), I have endeavoured: to show that this figure, Asura Maya, can be none other than an-Indian reminiscence of the Zoroastrian spirit, Ahura Mazda. That this confirms, in the most final way, the theory of the Persian character Of our palaces at Kumrahar is obvi- ous, but it is not of that matter that I wish to speak at present. In the Mahabhiarata account of these and similar royal and divine edifices, I found that particular emphasis is laid on structures denominated “ Sabhas,” which is t

I trenched elaborately in this direction to see if it least the débris of the rampart. would be traceable east of the seeming turning, but it could be followed only a little way. Then the wall appeared, with some uncertainty, to turn south again. The evidences of the blue clay confirm this inference. The rampart has apparently turned south again, and before we can follow. its eastward course further, more land, I fear, may have to be acquired, unless the consent of the owners can be obtained to exploration. On the north, at the edge of the terrace just south-west of the mound at Site No. II, whose position corre- sponds to that of the palace of Darius at Persepolis, we ‘have a layer of débris sloping outwards from the terrace (d.e., westwards) which appears analogous to the slope of débris on the south where we can see that it is the remmant of a rampart wall. Underneath this slope, moreover, we have the blue clay we had expected, and this we have followed for a little. Its eastern edge, which was what we were most anxious to determine, has been found a few feet within or to the east of the raised edge of the terrace on its western side. This is just where we had expected it, and the present indications are favourable to the assumption that it thence runs toward the south until it joing with the blue clay which we have reason to believe turns north under- neath the western side of the so-called “tank.” The monsoon broke, unfor- tunately, just after the pits had been outlined which aimed at determining the continuity of this clay from north to south, and until this continuity is cledrly established, it is impossible to speak with certainty. But blue clay has been found at one intermediate point, at least, and there is every reason to expect that the alignment will prove to be as has been indicated above, and that by following it in the manner described, we shall be able to draw the old original boundary of the terrace with exactitude. It will be satisfactory if this proves to be the case, for there is nothing left of the rampart over a considerable distance, and the recovery of its alignment inthis manner will be a fascinating undertaking. The main thing is, however, that we have already established the fact that there was a boundary to the palace area in ancient times. How minutely it agrees in alignment with the present edge of the modern terrace remains to be determined, but this is a matter of detail. Cultivation has demonstrably made encroachments here and there, as was to be expected. But speaking generally, and so far as present evidences go, there seems no doubt but what the modern configuration of the terrace does represent an ancient fact, and that that fact is in full harmony with our ex- pectations. This means to say that not only is the palace which we have partially | @x- cavated at Site No. I in close and detailed agreement with-its seeming. proto- type at Persepolis ; not only are the mounds adjacent to it in similar agree- ment with the corresponding members of the Persepolitan complex, but it is 54 now fairly certain that ‘all these buildings were ‘grouped, as at SPeeepane: within a definite confined space of generally similar configuration. ‘Thus such room for doubt of the Persepolitan theory as has existed heretofore is‘ dwind- ling markedly. ‘Lhe probability of its soundness has been materially increased. And therefore, although unfortunately it cannot be asserted that the final proof of its correctness has been recovered, real and definite progress has been made in the season under review, and that. alone is satisfactory. In these regards the little gem is very like the nose buttons in fashion at the present day, and the coolies had no hesitation in so designating it. The exquisite delicacy and perfection of its workmanship, however, show that it is not a product of the modern or any recent age. I should suppose that it could hard- ly be later than the second century, B. C., with a possibility of its being older still. Its form, too, is a point of interest, "for what could be more appropriate than this little golden i image of the sun at a site which is otherwise indicated so plainly as a centre of the Sun-worshippers ? But the most important confirmation of my Persian and Zoroastrian theory of the site found this year remains to mention. On the north of the so-called tank, near the place where the fragments of Mauryan images were found which we have just discussed, we came upon an extensive heap of ashes, the limits of which have not been ascertained. Among these ashes occur no end of potsherds, and many of these are decorated. Some have simple line ornaments and commonplace devices, others are more interesting. The latter class bears figures in relief, impressed upon them with a sort of seal or die, and these are not only prevailingly religious in character, but specifically Zoroastrian, so far as I can understand them. The most frequent: of these emblems is the Sun, which appears in a considerable variety of forms. One shows the rude tracing of a star (which is of importance since I claim that these are the places of the Danavas, and the Danavas are known as star-worshippers in Sanskrit literature), and in its association the conventional and almost heraldic, but very unmistakable, emblem of the Zoroastrian fire-altar. The figure is remarkably similar to that form of fire-altar which is shown on the fagde of Darius’s tomb at Persepalis, and which ig retained even into Sagsanian times in Persia, and appears on Sassanian coinage. The same devise has-been found at Vaisali and at Bhita on sealinzs, and we have even seen it among the seals recovered this year at this very site. But on our potsherds it appears in larger form and more detail, and I may addin more numerous examples. For we have some half dozen potsherds with this emblem. More striking confirmation of my theory of the Persian influence at Pataliputra could hardly be conceived. And when I add that I discovered, quite by accident, that the tract where they occur is still known to the local peasantry as Mauni Pokhar, the full significance of the find becomes apparent. dJ/auni is the Sanskrit word for a s¢lent men, and in the Bhavishya Purana, which describes the coming of the Magi to this country in late Epic times, this special term of Jfaunz is applied to them by way of nickname, the Hindus having dubbed them ‘Silentiaries’ because of their curious rule for eating in silence— a peculiarity which Sir Dorab Tata tells me is still maintained among the Parsis of the modern age. Mauni Pokhar, therefore, means ‘‘ The Magian’s Pool”, and it is doubly significant that such 2 name as this should be preserved by the -illiterate people of the neighbourhood, where all my other evidences have themselves so plainy pointed to the Magian character of the site, and- that in this very place, upon the edge, as it were, of this ‘‘ The Magian’s Pool’, we should have found this mass of sacred pottery with Zoroastrian emblems. Superintendent’s Programme for 1916-17.—Inasmuch as our field season has to be extended into the hot weather in Bihar, to permit of our reaching the lower levels in- our excavations, the compilation of this report is unavoidably delayed until well on into the new year. In June I had the honour of officiating as Director-General of Archeology in India during the short leave of Sir John Marshall. while Mr. Haranandan Panday acted in my stead as Superintendent and Assistant Superintendent and Officer-in-Charge of the Archeological Section of the Indian Museum in Calcutta. The month of July has been given to this report and the routine duties of my three offices. August I propose to devote to an inspection tour in the Central Provinces. September I hope can be given to the revision of the List of Ancient Monuments for Tirhut. October and November will afford opportunity for further touring in connexion with our conservation work, and thereafter I hope to resume the excavations at Nalanda and at the Bulandi Bagh, if not at other sites in Patna. It is of course for Sir Ratan Tata himself to say whether he wishes the Pataliputra excavations to be continued further at his expense. His wishes for artistic material have been sadly disappointed. Office.——As was recorded in paragraph 9 of my last year’s Report, the Superintendent was absent from this Circle for one month during the year 1916-17, (namely from the 5th June to tlie 4th July) while he officiated as Director General of Archeology, in the place of Sir John Marshall, then on leave. .Mr. Haranandan Panday, Excavation Assistant to the Director General, held charge of the offices of. both Superintendent and Assistant Superintendent during this period, and also of the Officer-in-Charge, Archeological Section, Indian Museum, Calcutta. ‘These three offices continued in the charge of one officer throughout the year, until the 21st December, 1916, when, by the appointment of Mr. Panday, the office of Assistant Superintendent was again filled. Thus the month of May was devoted to the Excavations at Nalanda, and the first two weeks of June were spent in Bankipore, where certain minor works were necessary in connexion with the Pataliputra Excavations, and where arrangements had to be made for my officiating term in Simla. To the latter place I proceeded on the 13th June, to take over charge of the Director Generalship for four months with effect from the 20th of that month, Mr. Charles Duroiselle coming from Burma to officiate in my stead as Superintendent i inthe Eastern Circle. On resuming charge at the end of October I now hope to devote myself actively for some six weeks or so to the revision of the List of Ancient Monuments and to placing various accumulated collections of Antiquities in the new Patna Museum. Somewhere about the first of the new year I hope to return to Nalanda for the further prosecution of our research work there; but, it is presumable that we shall have but a short season there this year. A certain amount of touring in connexion with our conservation work will also be inevitable, as occasion arises, but it is not easy at this time to foresee in detail where this may take nie. It is hoped also that the Tata Excavations at the Bulandi Bagh can be resumed next year, but the conditions of the site make it difficult to undertake this work until the approach of spring, as has been explained before. THE ROYAL ASIATIC SOGIETY'S EXCAVATIONS AT NALANDA. | ‘The preliminary account of the Nalanda excavations published in my Report for last year showed that our first trial trench had been led diagonally from south-east to north-west across the quadrangles numbered 2 and 1 on the plan published by Cunningham in volume I of his Archeological Survey Reports (facing page 28), and that after uncovering the north-west angle of quadrangle No. 1, We had focussed our attention upon the southern monastery numbered 2. Here the work carried out in the season of 1915-16 sufficed to give us the main dimensions of the monastic complex, 203 feet east and west and 168 feet north and south; to prove a frontage towards the west, with certain projections leading to a grand staircase on this side ; and to determine the existence of the main outer wall of this building still preserved to a height of some 24 feet when first disclosed. This main outer wall had at that time been examined only in one or two narrow cuttings, and I stated that whereas it then appeared to indicate a two-storeyed building, the cutting on the inside of the quadrangle disclosed reasons for suspecting that instead of one two-storeyed structure we were really concerned with two separate buildings, one built upon the other. ‘The evidences of the two sides of the wall thus seemed to be conflicting, and the real explanation of the problem was left for later settlement. EXCAVATIONS AT NALANDA, 1917-18. Exploration. Nalanda.—At the southern monastery at Nalanda, now denominated Site I, most of the additional clearance effected this year was outside the main walls. Thus the great bank of earth rising from the fields on the east and forming the eastern slope. of the mound was cut through from the top and cleared away from the east wall down to a depth of several feet below the high- est point of standing masonry, and the floor of the cutting so made was then levelled as a temporary roadway along this side of the monument. The same rocedure was followed also on the southern side, but here it was carried further than on the east.. That is to say, the cutting was made wider than in the for- mer instance, and when the general level, a little below the tops of the monas- tery wall, was cleared, alarge buttress was outlined in the centre of the south wall, with others at thé corners, east and west, and at intermediate points and subsequent : deepening. was restricted to the areas intervening between these buttresses. In this way a sufficient number of strong supports were left in the 40 enveloping soil as the digging proceeded to act as support to the masonry of the great southern wall, in case it proved to be bulged or otherwise weakened, as the work advanced; while a passage-way along this side of the monastery was also produced on the level of the deepening excavation. The work is. stiil in pro- gress, and a good deal of further clearance will be necessary before thesouth wall is set finally free. But before any much increased depth is attained, per- manent arrangements for drainage may prove to be unavoidable, both here and . on the west, where in the year under teview a beginning was made with the clearance of the southern half of the main facade. As all of this work was extramural, and seldom carried down to the final ground level, finds were of Course few and isolated. The lower depths may or may not yield more. Inside this monastery perhaps more attention was given to conservation this year than to further excavation; although the measures taken for the safeguarding of the remains during the previous monsoon had proved adequate for the time being. Further clearance was, hewever, effected to the northern half of the lower verandah on the east side, and to something like one half of the north verandah, beginning at the eastern end. In the preceding year this particular verandah, the fourth from the top, had appeared to be that of the original or oldest monastery on this site, with three later ones in successive ruins above it. A pit sunk in the south-east corner of this lowermost verandah this year, however, disclosed a still lower pavement five feet six inches lower down still, so that the successive existence of at least five monasteries on this one site can now be postulated confidently. It remains to be seen whether we can make any effective approach later on to this fifth or earliest structure, if indeed even it is the earliest. So far as our digging permitted us to judge (we were stopped finally by the accumulation of sub-soil water), we did not even eventu- ally get down into virgin soil, as stray potsherds were met with all along.

In the previous year we had cleared a portion of the north side of this greati mound, and had determined that there are at least three successive integuments of masonry, the oldest or innermost of which is still covered with a rather remarkably well-preserved stucco ornament, including several Buddha figures with attendants. This year the clearance was extended around the north-west angle and to the west side of the main monument, which was set free as far as the south-west ecrner. The Jatest .or outer integument here bears a terraced form, and is in places badly ruined. Whether this should be repaired, or whether it is here that we shoul] finally try to penetrate to the inner structures, can only be determined after the whole main monument has been cleared on all four sides, and we can see definitely where penetration - would involve least damage. Obviously the innermost stucco-coated building is both the oldest and the’ most important of the three so far determined. Whether it is the oldest at this site or not, we do no know. But although we | naturally desire to set as large a portion of this inner stupa, free as can be compassed, it is at the same time essential that only a minimum of disturbance ‘should occur to the later extensions. To guarantee the right procedure in so complicated a case, the first desideratum is to remove the enveloping earth on all sides. Then we can see exactly what the condition of the latest monument is in all its parts, and can avail ourselves of possible gaps here and there to approach the inner ones. The work is one of peculiar fascination, but rapid ‘progress is not advisable. So far as the main stupas are concerned, the succes- sive rebuildings have naturally and necessarily taken the form of outer integuments, so that, if I may so speak, the stratification of these several stages, is best shown in the horizontal plane. Excavation in the courtyards north and west however has disclosed a considerable number of small stupas clustering around the main cectral edifice in the usual way, but with, of course, a stratifi- cation running vertically. The west side of the great stupa is quite a mass of these little stupas, sometimes three on one and the same spot, one above another, with also evidence for a fourth or superimposed stratum of presumably very late date indeed. Rangamati.—tThis village of Rangamati (=coloured clay) is to be distinguished fromtwo other places (in Bengal) bearing the same name; one being the. town of Rangamati in the Murshidabad_ District, and the ‘other the village headquarters of the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Itis situated ‘at 26°19’ N. and 90° 36’ E. in the Gauripur Estate (Goalpara District) in the midst of a thick jungle of sal trees. In the latter half of the seventeenth cen- tury, during the wars between the Ahoms and the Emperor of Delhi, Rangamati was the headquarters of the Mughal Faujdar. The mosque, which is the most important of. these remains, stands on the top of a high hill inthe midst of a level piece of ground and occupies a commanding position overlooking the valley. The platform on which it is built, measures 96 feet long by 74 feet wide, with 34 feet of it in front of the mosque which is 68 feet in length by 28 feet in breadth, and about 32 feet high. Epigraphy.—The Government of Bengal forwarded to this office photo- graphs of the north and west walls of an inscrip- tion on the north wall of an ancient Hindu temple at Rainagar in the District of Jessore, and asked for a report on the inscrip- tion and the desirability of preserving the two walls with rather fine ornamen- tal brickwork, which is all that remains of the temple, The inscription is in rélief on bricks panelled on the northern wall, some of which have been Jost. The record consists of two verses in the Sanskyit language and Bengali script, and the date (Saka year 1510) written in Bengali figures in two places, The first verse is in praise of the God. Krishna, to whom the temple was in all probability dedicated, as is also apparent from the sculptural decorations on the west wall. The second gives the date and the name of the builder, who is mentioned as the son of Visvanatha. Pagan. During the year, an expenditure of R20,000 was incurred on repairs to several ancient pagodas at Pagan, viz., the Ananda, Thatbyinnyu, Manuha, Gawdawpalin, and Shwekugyi. The work done was of the nature of conservation, and consisted of uprooting jungle, making roofs water-tight, repairing cracked arches, and petty repairs to floors. The Ananda Pagoda (Plate XXIX) was built by King Kyanzittha in 1090 A.D. Its interior aisles are adorned with stone sculptures of exquisite workmanship, representing various scenes in the life of Buddha, while around the exterior walls of its four terraces are disposed in bands ornamental tile-work plaques, numbering some 1,500 in all, each of which illustrates a Buddhist ceremonial, or represents one of the Jātaka stories. It is intended to have photographs, or, if in some cases that is impracticable, draw- ings prepared of these plaques and to have the legend beneath carefully copied and translated, so that the Jātaka stories, which they illustrate, may, if possible, be identi- fied. Such a contribution to Buddhist iconography would, it is believed, be gladly welcomed and appreciated by Oriental scholars in Europe. " Thatbyinnyu" or "Sabbaññu" signifies "Omniscience," which is one of the attributes of Buddha. The pagoda of that name [Plate XXX(a)] was built by King Alaungsithu in 1144 A.D., after the model of Indian temples. It has five storeys: the first and second were used as the residence of monks; images were kept on the third; the fourth was used as a library; and on the fifth was constructed a pagoda containing holy relics. These revealed three distinct strata of brick structures: the uppermost belonging to the Muhammadan period, the second to the epoch of the Imperial Guptas, and the third to some more remote date. The Muhammadan remains are few and appear to be comparatively modern, while the lowest stratum is represented only by a few scattered fragments, too scanty to afford any conclusive evidence as to their precise date or character. It is in the remains of the Gupta era, therefore, that our interest mainly centres. These consist for the most part of small chambers standing little higher than their foundation, with floors of concrete and brick, while among the débris were found large numbers of the tiles with which their roofs were covered, together with terra cotta pinnacles and roughly carved bricks. The buildings are evidently of a secular nature throughout, and no remains of any temple have yet been brought to light; in fact, a miniature stone image of Gaṇeśa of later date was the only religious relic which turned up. This fact makes it all the more important for us to open up the whole group of buildings here, since no other structures of a similar character and of so early a date have yet been brought to light in India. The most interesting find made during the excavations consisted of a large num- ber of pieces of clay, bearing impressions of seals. The total amounted to about 720 pieces with somewhat over 1,100 seal-impressions on them. Among these are approxi- mately 120 varieties. Some seals occur very often, one (No. 29 in the following list) as many as 274 times. The place where this discovery was made has already been described above. The seals were found mixed up with fragments of pottery, burnt wood and rubbish inside a subterranean chamber, 10 feet square, in the north-western section of trench D. Evidently this room, which must have been closed over, and accessible only from above, served as a deposit for letters or similar documents, to which the seals had been attached, or it is also possible that it was used as a refuse chamber. A few seals, not more than ten, turned up here and there at different other places. They have been distinguished as such in the list. From the shape of the clay pieces it is evident that they were attached to letters or other literary documents, and that they served to hold together the string which was tied around the wooden boards, upon which the letter was writ- ten, or which were used as a sort of envelope. In that case either birch- bark or palm-leaf took the place of our modern paper. Fig. 18 gives a view of the reverse of one of the clay lumps. The method adopted for sealing letters at this time seems to have been to press down the ends of the string tied round the boards into a piece of moist clay by means of some instrument, perhaps the broad side of a knife. Evidence of this is the groove which invariably occurs on the back of all the seals. Generally a few thin lines run across its centre. They must have been made by the blunt edge of the knife to press down the strings more deeply, in order to make them adhere tighter to the clay. The other side of Full size. The plate attached to it is written in characters of the 9th or 10th century A.D, approximately, while the legend of the seal (Kumārāmātyādhikaraṇasya) is in the alphabet of the early Gupta kings The plate appears to contain a grant made by a person who held the office of Kumārāmātyādhikaraṇa. To the left hand side of the figure of Lakṣmi is the impression of another small seal, about inch in diameter, with the figure of a boar and the legend: Śrī Lokanathasya, in characters of the same type as the copper-plate inscription. If the inscription of the plate is not a mere forgery, which I am unable to decide at present, we should find an officer of the rank of Kumārāmātyādhikaraṇa continuing to enjoy a certain amount of territorial independence in a remote district of the East several centuries after the period of the early Gupta kings. In a recent note published in the Journal of the German Oriental Society (Vol. LVIII, page 867), Professor Lüders refers to a prelimi- nary notice on the discovery of the theatre in the Sitābengā cave, published by me in the same Volume on page 455. He first points to certain passages in Kālidāsa's poems, which, however phantastical, show that caves in ancient India were not entirely built for anchorites, but often served quite different purposes as the abode of dancing girls and their lovers, and he very ingeniously explains the word leṇaśobhikā " cave actress." The Greek influence often stretches very far in India, and in time, I believe, we shall be able to trace it much farther than we think at present The well-known statue of Apollo carved upon one of the relic pillars at Budh-Gaya has become the prototype of the later Indian representations of Surya. It is shown on Plate L of Mitra's Buddha Gaya, and a similar figure is found inside the Ananta Cave in the Khandagiri Hill in Orissa. The makara of Kāma looks like a certain adoption of the Dolphin of Eros, and upon the coping stones of the Bharhut railing we find the figure of a bull having the head of a bearded man, unfortunately left out in Cunningham's photographs, in which we may easily recognize an imitation of the Greek river-gods, so common on Greek coins, whatever idea the Bharhut sculptor may have associated with this design These are only a few instances of Greek influence on Indian Art. The amphi- theatre in front of the Sitābengā Cave also forms a link in the same chain, and its bearings upon the literary side of the question of Greek influence in the Indian drama cannot be overlooked.
